responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark faces a structural sovereignty and resilience crisis: MitID's dependence on Apple and Google platform integrity signals leaves critical public authentication vulnerable to foreign vendor decisions, policy shifts, or geopolitical disruption. The project's core tension is between the regulatory conservatism and certification burden of the incumbent MitID ecosystem and the urgency of establishing platform-neutral alternatives before AltID hardens the same dependencies. Success requires navigating three competing pressures: technical credibility (demonstrators must prove fallback authentication is feasible without looking like prototype theater), institutional capture (Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the MitID operator have incentives to avoid disruption), and political timing (EU eIDAS2 harmonization creates a narrow window for procurement language changes before national implementations lock in). The selected levers target supplier concentration risk, procurement intervention before design hardens, coalition strength to counter incumbent resistance, and demonstrator credibility to make fallback paths politically defensible.

levers.name: Demonstrator Scope and Platform Choice
levers.consequences: Selecting between a privacy-respecting Android fork (GrapheneOS), a browser-based fallback, or a hardware-token pathway determines technical defensibility and adoption feasibility for phase two. A GrapheneOS demonstrator proves mobile-parity without proprietary platform APIs but narrows audience to privacy-conscious adopters; browser-based or token approaches widen access but may appear less integrated into citizen workflows. The choice cascades into phase three messaging: narrow technical proof-of-concept invites dismissal as niche, while overly broad scope risks feature creep and missed credibility deadlines.
options: Develop a single tightly-scoped FIDO2/WebAuthn mobile demonstrator on GrapheneOS authenticated against a simulated Danish identity provider, prioritizing protocol compliance and security review over feature parity with MitID's convenience features, to establish that standards-based fallback authentication is technically sound without expanding scope into production-readiness.

Build dual lightweight demonstrators in parallel—a GrapheneOS-based mobile pathway and a browser-plus-hardware-token fallback—each addressing a distinct citizen segment (technical users and accessibility-first users), then measure relative institutional and policy traction to inform phase three procurement language.

Pursue a web-only fallback demonstrator using standard OIDC and FIDO2 without mobile OS dependence, accepting reduced seamlessness with mobile banking workflows but gaining immediate browser compatibility and lower implementation friction for citizens using older or non-standard devices.
levers.review_lever: Mobile-centric designs risk appearing too niche; browser-only fallbacks may seem too distant from citizens' primary authentication patterns. All three options fail to address the specific approval and integration mechanics that Digitaliseringsstyrelsen would require before accepting any fallback into actual procurement—demonstrators prove feasibility, not institutional readiness.

levers.name: Coalition Composition and Advocacy Timing
levers.consequences: Phase one must secure visible support from civil-society, academic, and security-expert voices to reframe the issue from ideology to resilience and contingency risk. Early endorsement from privacy advocates and cybersecurity researchers increases credibility with EU-level standards bodies; early parliamentary engagement (Folketinget's digital policy committee) signals political viability. However, coalition-building takes time and competing agendas often dilute unified messaging. Timing the coalition announcement too early risks incumbent preemption; too late risks appearing reactive after AltID design decisions have begun hardening.
options: Build coalition sequentially, beginning with academic and security researchers in months 1–3 to establish technical credibility, then adding parliamentary and civil-society voices in months 4–6 to frame the political and resilience narrative, creating cumulative visible support that peaks during phase one's final deliverable publication.

Convene coalition members simultaneously across all constituencies in month 1, accepting coordination overhead and initial message variance, to establish unified public-facing pressure on Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the MitID operator before they begin AltID design specification work.

Cultivate a deliberately lean coalition of 4–6 strategic institutional actors (including one sympathetic Digitaliseringsstyrelsen contact and one respected security researcher) who meet privately to co-author and co-sign phase one outputs, maximizing insider influence and decision-maker proximity at the cost of visible grassroots perception.
levers.review_lever: Sequential building creates credibility momentum but risks timing misalignment with AltID's unannounced design gates; simultaneous convening dilutes focus; insider-only coalition maximizes procurement influence but forfeits grassroots legitimacy and EU-level narrative power. None address how to sustain coalition cohesion across the 24-month project if early wins are muted or procurement language is adopted without binding commitment.

levers.name: Platform-Neutrality Language in Procurement and Standards
levers.consequences: Phase three's success hinges on inserting binding language into AltID procurement, eIDAS2 guidelines, or EU Digital Identity Wallet standards requiring platform-neutral access and certified fallback paths. If language appears only in consultation documents or advisory frameworks, it carries minimal enforcement weight and incumbent operators can dismiss it as non-binding. If procurement language is concrete and tied to future funding or certification gates, it creates real friction for MitID-incumbent design—but only if Digitaliseringsstyrelsen or EU bodies perceive platform concentration as a contingency risk worth operationalizing.
options: Propose explicit negative procurement requirements stating that AltID and successor identity systems shall not depend exclusively on Apple iOS or Google Android app stores, push-notification infrastructure, or proprietary platform integrity APIs, making platform monopoly a disqualifying architectural choice.

Draft interoperability and portability clauses in AltID specifications requiring that any approved authentication pathway must remain functional across at least two independent device ecosystems or via a non-mobile fallback, without naming Apple or Google but creating structural incentive for fallback design.

Advocate for a "contingency authentication" track within EU Digital Identity Wallet materials, framing fallback mechanisms as mandatory resilience features for critical public services, and then reference this EU-level language in Danish procurement to avoid direct confrontation with incumbent operators.
levers.review_lever: Direct negative requirements risk legal challenge by platform vendors and political backlash from MitID operator as sovereignty infringement; interoperability clauses are softer but easy to satisfy with cosmetic changes; EU-level framing delegates authority but sacrifices Danish-level urgency and may not translate into binding national procurement terms.

levers.name: Institutional Engagement and Decision-Gate Mapping
levers.consequences: Phase one must identify the specific regulatory bodies, approval hierarchies, and decision gates controlling AltID design, eIDAS certification, and continued MitID funding. Early engagement with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen and the MitID operator clarifies which stakeholders perceive platform concentration as a risk and which view fallback authentication as a threat to incumbent market position. Mapping approval timelines and blockers reveals whether procurement language can influence design before sign-off deadlines—if AltID design freezes in month 12 and phase three engagement begins in month 17, institutional traction becomes speculative.
options: Conduct formal structured interviews with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, the MitID operator, relevant authorities (Statens IT), and at least two EU-connected digital identity working groups in months 2–4, document decision gates and approval timelines explicitly, and publish a stakeholder map showing which actors have veto power over platform-neutral requirements.

Propose a formal advisory working group co-convened by the project and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, meeting quarterly throughout the project to review feasibility findings and align on procurement language in real time, trading autonomy for insider access and reducing risk of phase three irrelevance.

Identify a single sympathetic decision-maker within Digitaliseringsstyrelsen or the MitID operator in month 1, build a confidential relationship, and use that person as a feedback loop and early-warning channel for policy windows and institutional friction, maximizing responsiveness but risking perception of capture if the relationship becomes visible.
levers.review_lever: Structured interviews produce public documentation but may encounter resistance or vague responses if stakeholders perceive the project as challenging incumbent interests; advisory working group guarantees access but obligates the project to soften criticism; confidential insider relationships maximize intelligence but collapse credibility if exposed and leave no institutional record of engagement.

levers.name: External Security Review and Credibility Gatekeeping
levers.consequences: Phase two demonstrators must withstand scrutiny from EU and Danish security authorities, eIDAS assessors, and incumbent operators looking for reasons to dismiss fallback authentication as inferior or inadequately audited. Engaging an independent third-party security reviewer (either an accredited evaluation facility or a respected external research group) strengthens phase two deliverables and inoculates the project against dismissal as technically naive. However, external review is expensive, adds schedule risk (reviewers have their own backlogs), and may surface implementation gaps that require rework—and reviewers can become bottlenecks if they withhold findings or demand changes that conflict with phase three messaging goals.
options: Procure a formal security evaluation from an accredited Common Criteria or eIDAS-qualified evaluation facility in months 10–14, targeting a published assessment report that speaks the language of procurement reviewers and regulators, accepting 4–6 week schedule contingency and significant budget allocation.

Engage a respected open-source security community (e.g., an established FIDO2 or WebAuthn maintainer, or a recognized academic security lab) to review phase two code and architecture in months 11–15, trading formal certification authority for perceived independence and community legitimacy.

Conduct an internal security review led by the project's own mobile security researcher, supplemented by one day of external audit from a freelance security consultant, reducing cost and schedule risk but creating reputational vulnerability if reviewers later identify gaps that stakeholders attribute to insufficient external rigor.
levers.review_lever: Formal evaluation maximizes procurement credibility but adds cost and schedule risk; community review carries legitimacy but lacks formal eIDAS standing; internal review minimizes friction but invites dismissal as self-serving if demonstrators face later criticism. None guarantee that security findings will support (rather than undermine) phase three procurement advocacy.

levers.name: Fallback Scope Definition and Continuity Scenario
levers.consequences: A platform-neutral fallback must define its intended use case: is it a daily-use alternative to MitID, a contingency-only path activated when platform policies change, a accessibility feature for citizens unable to use proprietary OSes, or a resilience hedge against geopolitical disruption? The definition determines technical requirements, integration depth, and regulatory burden. A daily-use alternative requires parity with MitID's convenience and must compete against incumbent adoption advantages, creating an adoption cliff. A contingency-only path can remain lightweight and unintegrated but risks perception as a theoretical exercise if it is never activated. The choice also determines which stakeholders feel threatened: a daily-use fallback threatens MitID operator and platform vendors; a contingency path threatens only vendors' strategic lock-in but may satisfy regulatory skeptics.
options: Define the fallback as a standby contingency pathway activated only upon triggering conditions (platform policy change, geopolitical sanctions, certification failure, or MitID operator bankruptcy), explicitly not targeting daily-use adoption, and anchor phase two demonstrators and phase three procurement language around continuity-of-service resilience rather than competitive feature parity.

Position the fallback as a first-class daily-use alternative requiring feature and convenience parity with MitID (secure passwordless authentication, biometric unlock, push notifications, banking integration), accepting that phase two demonstrators will reveal significant integration friction and phase three will face resistance from both MitID operator and platform vendors.

Propose a hybrid model in which the fallback authenticates citizens for non-time-critical public services (tax filing, healthcare portals, administrative records) while MitID retains banking and high-security transactions, carving out a protected niche for fallback growth without directly competing for MitID's core revenue and regulatory value.
levers.review_lever: Contingency-only framing avoids incumbent resistance but appears self-limiting and may be discounted as academic if never invoked; daily-use parity requires feature completeness that phase two demonstrators are unlikely to deliver; hybrid positioning creates a two-tier authentication landscape that may confuse citizens and fragments regulatory oversight. All three options leave unaddressed how to define the technical and legal 'activation trigger' that would justify switching citizens to a fallback path mid-deployment.

levers.name: EU-Level Standards Alignment and Transnational Messaging
levers.consequences: Phase three includes EU-level engagement with European Digital Identity Wallet working groups and eIDAS2 harmonization bodies. If Denmark's platform-neutrality advocacy aligns with concurrent EU-wide pressure for interoperability and reduced vendor lock-in, the project gains regulatory authority and reduces perception of Denmark as isolated or ideological. However, EU harmonization timelines often lag national procurement cycles, and EU working groups operate by consensus—a single large-member veto (e.g., from a state heavily invested in a specific platform vendor) can dilute language to non-binding aspiration. Conversely, if Denmark moves unilaterally and EU bodies later adopt conflicting standards, the project's procurement language risks obsolescence or contradiction.
options: Monitor concurrent EU Digital Identity Wallet and eIDAS2 working-group activity closely from month 1, and time phase three EU engagement (months 17–24) to directly feed project findings into working groups that are actively drafting specifications, maximizing influence on emerging EU-level language while aligning Danish procurement with harmonized standards.

Propose a formal joint working arrangement with an established EU-level standards body (e.g., ENISA or a eIDAS2 technical working group) in phase one, securing a seat for the project's regulatory specialist and making EU-level engagement continuous throughout the project, trading coordination overhead for upstream influence on EU specifications.

Execute Denmark-first procurement language in phase three independently, then use that language and the demonstrators as a proof-of-concept to advocate for similar EU-level requirements in month 20–24, positioning Denmark as a leadership exemplar rather than waiting for EU consensus to emerge.
levers.review_lever: Monitoring and timing requires accurate prediction of EU body activity and risks chasing a moving target; formal joint arrangements with EU bodies add coordination complexity but guarantee venue; Denmark-first approach maximizes autonomy but risks regulatory misalignment if EU standards diverge. None address how to manage political friction if EU bodies reject or dilute language that Denmark has already embedded in procurement.

levers.name: Budget Contingency and Phase-Gate Discipline
levers.consequences: The project is budgeted at 10.5 million DKK across three phases with conditional funding (phase two and three are gated on phase one deliverables and institutional engagement). If phase one overruns or delivers weak institutional engagement, phase two funding becomes vulnerable to reallocation or cancellation, eliminating the demonstrators that provide proof-of-concept for phase three. Conversely, if phase two demonstrators succeed rapidly and phase three institutional traction appears strong, stakeholders may pressure scope expansion (production-readiness, feature richness, rapid pilot deployment) that exceeds the remaining budget and delays phase three messaging work. Budget discipline requires either strict gating (refusing scope expansion and deferring features to out-of-scope future phases) or explicit contingency reserve allocation (retaining 10–15% of budget unallocated until phase three to respond to emergent institutional opportunities).
options: Enforce strict conditional funding gates with published phase-exit criteria (phase one: published feasibility report + formal stakeholder engagement letter + documented financing plan; phase two: working demonstrators + independent security review + positive feedback from at least one regulatory stakeholder), refusing scope expansion and deferring feature requests to a post-project roadmap.

Allocate a 1.5 million DKK contingency reserve held by the project lead outside the formal phase budgets, enabling rapid response to emergent institutional opportunities (e.g., a surprise EU working-group request, an unexpected Digitaliseringsstyrelsen receptiveness, or demonstrator findings requiring urgent follow-up analysis) without derailing primary phase deliverables.

Structure phase funding with explicit overrun tolerance (e.g., allow phase one to consume up to 3.5 million DKK if institutional engagement requires additional stakeholder meetings), then correspondingly reduce phase two or three scope, making trade-offs explicit rather than hidden or deferred.
levers.review_lever: Strict gating minimizes scope creep but may miss high-leverage institutional opportunities that require immediate response; contingency reserve adds complexity and governance risk; flexible overrun tolerance makes budgets soft and phase three scope unclear. None prevent the scenario in which phase three arrives with credible demonstrators but insufficient budget for sustained procurement influence over a 6–8 month policy window.

responses.strategic_rationale: Denmark's digital identity system faces structural supplier concentration risk—MitID's trust model depends on Apple and Google platform signals for fraud prevention and app integrity across banking, tax, and healthcare access. The project must navigate three interlocking tensions: (1) technical credibility without attempting a production-replacement system; (2) institutional influence over AltID procurement without direct authority over the process; (3) coalition-building across civil society, academia, and government stakeholders with conflicting incentives and timelines. The selected levers prioritize resilience framing and standards pressure over direct technical disruption, emphasize phase-gate discipline to avoid budget creep, and establish fallback continuity scenarios that reduce reliance on incumbent operator cooperation.

levers.name: Demonstrator Maturity and Certification Pathway
levers.consequences: Building non-production demonstrators on GrapheneOS or comparable platforms proves technical feasibility of standards-based authentication without Apple/Google dependency, but raises institutional expectations about production readiness and may trigger premature demand for full MitID compatibility testing. The choice of target certification level (eIDAS2 Substantial versus lower assurance) directly affects both credibility with regulators and scope creep during phase two.
options: Develop two separate demonstrators—one mobile-centric on GrapheneOS achieving eIDAS Substantial-level assurance through external security review, and one browser-based fallback requiring only browser APIs and no OS-level trust signals—to establish that platform-neutral paths exist at different assurance tiers without forcing a single unified architecture.

Build a single integrated demonstrator targeting eIDAS Substantial certification and seeking formal European Digital Identity Wallet compatibility testing, accepting longer timelines and higher technical overhead in exchange for direct regulatory recognition and clearer EU-level standards alignment.

Prioritize a minimalist hardware-token-based fallback demonstrator (FIDO2 over NFC or USB) that deliberately avoids mobile OS dependency entirely, trading off ease-of-citizen-use for absolute clarity that the fallback path is genuinely independent of Apple, Google, and future platform policy changes.
levers.review_lever: Demonstrator scope directly trades maturity against speed; the unaddressed gap is how to prevent phase-two scope creep when institutional stakeholders conflate demonstrator feasibility with deployment-readiness.

levers.name: Resilience Framing Versus Platform-Neutrality Language
levers.consequences: Emphasizing supplier-concentration risk, continuity-of-service exposure, and contingency-planning rationales (rather than anti-platform ideology or privacy critique) appeals to risk-management stakeholders and procurement authorities, but may dilute the underlying digital-sovereignty argument and cede moral authority to incumbent operators who claim they are already resilient. The framing choice shapes which coalitions mobilize and which institutional decision-makers feel empowered to act.
options: Lead with supplier-concentration and geopolitical-contingency risk language in all policy documents and procurement engagement, positioning platform neutrality as a necessary consequence of resilience rather than an ideological goal, and restrict digital-sovereignty framing to internal coalition communications and civil-society audiences.

Maintain parallel messaging—resilience and contingency arguments for institutional and procurement stakeholders, combined with explicit digital-sovereignty and democratic-accountability arguments in parallel public and EU-facing communications—accepting the complexity cost of message coherence in exchange for broader coalition appeal.

Anchor the entire project narrative on a single formal risk assessment (e.g., 'Danish Digital Identity Contingency and Supplier Concentration Report') published in month three of phase one, establishing a neutral, evidence-based baseline that all subsequent messaging and coalition engagement references, reducing the perception of selective framing.
levers.review_lever: Resilience framing gains institutional traction but may obscure sovereignty concerns; the unaddressed gap is whether contingency risk alone justifies major architectural changes absent an acute crisis.

levers.name: AltID Engagement Timing and Influence Depth
levers.consequences: AltID's eIDAS2 wallet rollout creates a design window where platform-neutral requirements can be incorporated before the next identity stack hardens incumbent dependencies, but the rollout timeline may not align with this project's phase gates, and the project has no formal authority over AltID's architecture. Early engagement risks being dismissed as premature; late engagement finds decisions already locked in. The depth of sought influence (advisory input versus formal procurement language) affects both political feasibility and institutional resistance.
options: Pursue formal procurement advisory-board or technical working-group membership in AltID from month six onward, positioning the project as a standards and resilience expert and building incremental influence over months 12–20 when wallet design decisions crystallize, accepting slower formal traction in exchange for sustainable institutional presence.

Submit a detailed 'platform-neutral procurement requirements' white paper to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen by month four, styled as formal policy input rather than advocacy, with the explicit goal of shaping the AltID procurement RFP language before month eight, accepting higher institutional friction if the proposal is perceived as prescriptive rather than consultative.

Deliberately de-couple from AltID decision timelines in phase two and three; instead, anchor the project's influence through EU-level eIDAS2 wallet harmonization working groups and standards bodies, positioning Danish advocacy as part of broader European resilience and interoperability discussions, with the expectation that EU-level requirements cascade back into Danish procurement by month 20–24.
levers.review_lever: Early AltID engagement risks dismissal; late engagement misses the design window; the unaddressed gap is how to time influence when AltID's own decision schedule and phase-gate discipline are unknown.

levers.name: Coalition Cohesion and Incentive Alignment
levers.consequences: Building a coalition spanning civil-society privacy advocates, security researchers, contingency-planning stakeholders, and sympathetic Folketinget members creates political credibility and distributed influence, but members have competing priorities: privacy advocates prioritize data protection, security researchers prioritize technical standards, and government insiders prioritize procurement speed. Disagreement over messaging, timeline, or technical detail can fragment the coalition and reduce institutional impact.
options: Establish a formal steering committee with written charter (month two) defining decision rules, messaging guidelines, and escalation paths, with rotating lead responsibility across constituencies (civil society lead months 2–8, researcher lead months 9–16, government-liaison lead months 17–24), ensuring no single faction dominates and incentives remain aligned.

Create three sub-coalitions around distinct outcomes: a technical standards group focused on eIDAS harmonization, a resilience and contingency group focused on supplier-concentration risk, and a digital-sovereignty and democratic-accountability group focused on public messaging, allowing each to operate semi-autonomously while coordinating through monthly cross-group briefings.

Keep the coalition loosely federated with only an informal coordination email list and monthly video calls, avoiding formal governance overhead and reducing the risk of bureaucratic friction or decision paralysis, but establish a lead partner organization (e.g., the project's host institution) as the binding anchor for continuity if individual members' priorities shift.
levers.review_lever: Formal governance ensures alignment but introduces overhead and reduces coalition flexibility; informal coordination avoids bureaucracy but risks fragmentation when priorities diverge.

levers.name: External Security Review and Public Credibility
levers.consequences: Engaging a recognized external security firm or academic lab to review the demonstrators and feasibility work before phase-three publication establishes technical credibility with regulators and incumbent operators, but external review adds 8–12 weeks and significant cost (typically 0.5–1.0 million DKK), and reviewers may flag contingencies or limitations that complicate procurement advocacy. The timing and scope of review (demonstrators only, versus full feasibility report, versus ongoing assurance) directly affects both cost and institutional weight.
options: Commission a formal security assessment of both demonstrators by an internationally recognized firm (e.g., a Big Four auditor or top-tier security lab) in months 13–15, timed to completion before phase-three procurement engagement, and explicitly publish the assessment (redacted only for operational security) to create a third-party credibility barrier against incumbent operator dismissal.

Arrange a series of rolling peer reviews and expert workshops (months 10–18) with invited security researchers, eIDAS compliance experts, and MitID operators themselves, documenting all feedback in a transparent 'responses to expert input' document rather than commissioning a single formal report, reducing cost while building apparent institutional buy-in.

Delay external review until month 20, after demonstrators are complete and the feasibility report is drafted, allowing the project to incorporate early internal feedback and reduce the scope of formal review to validation of claimed technical properties rather than full architecture assessment, reducing cost and timeline risk at the expense of delayed institutional credibility.
levers.review_lever: Early formal review builds credibility but adds cost and timeline pressure; late review reduces cost but delays credibility when institutional decisions are already made.

levers.name: Institutional Overhead and Workspace Governance
levers.consequences: The project requires a physical base in Copenhagen with access-controlled workspace appropriate for security-sensitive digital identity research and stakeholder meetings. Workspace type (dedicated facility versus distributed office space), governance model (project-controlled versus host-institution-controlled), and overhead allocation (separate budget line versus absorbed by host institution) directly affect both operational security and budget predictability. Insufficient overhead planning creates friction in month 8–10 when phase-two demonstrator work intensifies and stakeholder access and document-control requirements become critical.
options: Establish a dedicated, access-controlled research facility (leased or hosted at a single Copenhagen institution) under project governance, with formal document-classification protocols, visitor sign-in, and segregated demonstration-environment infrastructure, incurring approximately 0.6–0.8 million DKK over 24 months in overhead, but ensuring operational security and reducing dependence on host-institution administrative capacity.

Negotiate embedded workspace within the host institution's existing secure research or innovation facility, operating under host-institution security policies and governance, reducing dedicated overhead to approximately 0.2–0.3 million DKK (utilities and local staffing support) but accepting delays in decisions or access changes if host-institution priorities shift.

Distribute team members across multiple institutional locations (university labs, independent research facility, temporary co-working spaces for meetings) without a single dedicated facility, minimizing overhead cost but requiring explicit remote-work protocols, encrypted document repositories, and scheduled in-person coordination windows (e.g., bi-weekly meetings in Copenhagen), increasing operational friction and coordination overhead.
levers.review_lever: Dedicated facility ensures security and operational control but adds fixed cost; distributed model reduces overhead but increases coordination friction during demonstrator development.

levers.name: EU Standards Alignment and Temporal Scope of Advocacy
levers.consequences: Engaging European Digital Identity Wallet working groups and eIDAS2 harmonization forums (months 10–24) can amplify Danish procurement influence by aligning it with broader EU resilience and interoperability requirements, but European standards development is slow and outcomes are uncertain, and linking the project's success criteria to EU-level language creates dependency on processes outside the project's control. The choice of whether to pursue EU engagement in parallel with or sequentially after Danish institutional engagement directly affects both timeline risk and credibility positioning.
options: Initiate EU-level standards engagement in month six (parallel with phase-one feasibility work), positioning Denmark as a leading voice on platform-neutral resilience and interoperability, with the explicit goal of contributing language to official European Digital Identity Wallet materials by month 20, accepting longer timelines and lower certainty of Danish procurement impact in exchange for broader strategic influence.

Pursue Danish institutional and AltID engagement intensively in phase two and early phase three (months 9–20), and only if that engagement shows weak traction by month 16 pivot to EU-level standards forums as a secondary channel for influence, reducing timeline risk for Danish outcomes but potentially arriving at EU forums too late to shape emerging standards documents.

Focus exclusively on Danish procurement and institutional influence in all three phases, treating EU-level engagement as coordination and information-sharing (attending working groups but not leading initiatives), and measure success on Danish outcomes alone, accepting that broader European impact is uncertain but reducing the project's exposure to external standards-development timelines.
levers.review_lever: Early EU engagement amplifies voice but creates timeline dependency on slow European processes; the unaddressed gap is how to sequence Danish institutional impact and EU influence without diluting effort across two parallel tracks.

levers.name: Phase-Gate Contingency and Scope De-Escalation Triggers
levers.consequences: The project is gated at months 8 and 16, with conditional funding and explicit scope-reduction language ('if formal traction with AltID is weak by month 16, phase three should de-scope'). This discipline prevents budget overrun and scope creep but requires defining operationally clear triggers for de-escalation (e.g., 'no written response from Digitaliseringsstyrelsen by month 10' or 'demonstrator completion delayed beyond month 15') and committing to actual scope cuts when triggers are met. Weak trigger definitions or decision-maker reluctance to enforce scope cuts undermines the entire phase-gate model.
options: Establish formal, publicly documented phase-gate criteria in month one (e.g., 'phase two funding requires publication of feasibility report AND documented meeting with at least two Digitaliseringsstyrelsen stakeholders AND completion of 80 percent of phase-one deliverables by week 32'), with explicit approval authority and escalation path if criteria are not met, accepting governance overhead in exchange for credible commitment to phase gates.

Maintain flexible gate criteria reviewed monthly by the project steering committee, with criteria adjusted if emerging circumstances (e.g., unexpected government transition, AltID timeline change) warrant, reducing rigid bureaucracy but requiring strong governance discipline and clear decision rules for when adjustments are legitimate versus when they represent scope creep.

Define a single hard trigger for phase-three scope reduction ('if AltID procurement decision is finalized before month 14, phase three shifts entirely to EU-level standards and publication work, with no attempt to influence Danish procurement'), and commit that all other phase-gate reviews are advisory rather than funding-contingent, reducing decision burden but risking institutional drift if phase-one or phase-two deliverables are weak.
levers.review_lever: Formal gates prevent scope creep but require discipline in execution; the unaddressed gap is defining objective triggers that distinguish legitimate scope adjustment from gate-breaking scope expansion.

options: Conduct formal structured interviews with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, the MitID operator, relevant authorities (Statens IT), and at least two EU-connected digital identity working groups in months 2–4, document decision gates and approval timelines explicitly, and publish a stakeholder map showing which actors have veto power over platform-neutral requirements.

Propose a formal advisory working group co-convened by the project and Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, meeting quarterly throughout the project to review feasibility findings and align on procurement language in real time, trading autonomy for insider access and reducing risk of phase three irrelevance.

Identify a single sympathetic decision-maker within Digitaliseringsstyrelsen or the MitID operator in month 1, build a confidential relationship, and use that person as a feedback loop and early-warning channel for policy windows and institutional friction, maximizing responsiveness but risking perception of capture if the relationship becomes visible.
levers.review: Structured interviews produce public documentation but may encounter resistance or vague responses if stakeholders perceive the project as challenging incumbent interests; advisory working group guarantees access but obligates the project to soften criticism; confidential insider relationships maximize intelligence but collapse credibility if exposed and leave no institutional record of engagement.

levers.name: External Security Review and Credibility Gatekeeping
levers.consequences: Phase two demonstrators must withstand scrutiny from EU and Danish security authorities, eIDAS assessors, and incumbent operators looking for reasons to dismiss fallback authentication as inferior or inadequately audited. Engaging an independent third-party security reviewer (either an accredited evaluation facility or a respected external research group) strengthens phase two deliverables and inoculates the project against dismissal as technically naive. However, external review is expensive, adds schedule risk (reviewers have their own backlogs), and may surface implementation gaps that require rework—and reviewers can become bottlenecks if they withhold findings or demand changes that conflict with phase three messaging goals.
options: Procure a formal security evaluation from an accredited Common Criteria or eIDAS-qualified evaluation facility in months 10–14, targeting a published assessment report that speaks the language of procurement reviewers and regulators, accepting 4–6 week schedule contingency and significant budget allocation.

Engage a respected open-source security community (e.g., an established FIDO2 or WebAuthn maintainer, or a recognized academic security lab) to review phase two code and architecture in months 11–15, trading formal certification authority for perceived independence and community legitimacy.

Conduct an internal security review led by the project's own mobile security researcher, supplemented by one day of external audit from a freelance security consultant, reducing cost and schedule risk but creating reputational vulnerability if reviewers later identify gaps that stakeholders attribute to insufficient external rigor.
levers.review: Formal evaluation maximizes procurement credibility but adds cost and schedule risk; community review carries legitimacy but lacks formal eIDAS standing; internal review minimizes friction but invites dismissal as self-serving if demonstrators face later criticism. None guarantee that security findings will support (rather than undermine) phase three procurement advocacy.

levers.name: Fallback Scope Definition and Continuity Scenario
levers.consequences: A platform-neutral fallback must define its intended use case: is it a daily-use alternative to MitID, a contingency-only path activated when platform policies change, a accessibility feature for citizens unable to use proprietary OSes, or a resilience hedge against geopolitical disruption? The definition determines technical requirements, integration depth, and regulatory burden. A daily-use alternative requires parity with MitID's convenience and must compete against incumbent adoption advantages, creating an adoption cliff. A contingency-only path can remain lightweight and unintegrated but risks perception as a theoretical exercise if it is never activated. The choice also determines which stakeholders feel threatened: a daily-use fallback threatens MitID operator and platform vendors; a contingency path threatens only vendors' strategic lock-in but may satisfy regulatory skeptics.
options: Define the fallback as a standby contingency pathway activated only upon triggering conditions (platform policy change, geopolitical sanctions, certification failure, or MitID operator bankruptcy), explicitly not targeting daily-use adoption, and anchor phase two demonstrators and phase three procurement language around continuity-of-service resilience rather than competitive feature parity.

Position the fallback as a first-class daily-use alternative requiring feature and convenience parity with MitID (secure passwordless authentication, biometric unlock, push notifications, banking integration), accepting that phase two demonstrators will reveal significant integration friction and phase three will face resistance from both MitID operator and platform vendors.

Propose a hybrid model in which the fallback authenticates citizens for non-time-critical public services (tax filing, healthcare portals, administrative records) while MitID retains banking and high-security transactions, carving out a protected niche for fallback growth without directly competing for MitID's core revenue and regulatory value.
levers.review: Contingency-only framing avoids incumbent resistance but appears self-limiting and may be discounted as academic if never invoked; daily-use parity requires feature completeness that phase two demonstrators are unlikely to deliver; hybrid positioning creates a two-tier authentication landscape that may confuse citizens and fragments regulatory oversight. All three options leave unaddressed how to define the technical and legal 'activation trigger' that would justify switching citizens to a fallback path mid-deployment.

levers.name: EU-Level Standards Alignment and Transnational Messaging
levers.consequences: Phase three includes EU-level engagement with European Digital Identity Wallet working groups and eIDAS2 harmonization bodies. If Denmark's platform-neutrality advocacy aligns with concurrent EU-wide pressure for interoperability and reduced vendor lock-in, the project gains regulatory authority and reduces perception of Denmark as isolated or ideological. However, EU harmonization timelines often lag national procurement cycles, and EU working groups operate by consensus—a single large-member veto (e.g., from a state heavily invested in a specific platform vendor) can dilute language to non-binding aspiration. Conversely, if Denmark moves unilaterally and EU bodies later adopt conflicting standards, the project's procurement language risks obsolescence or contradiction.
options: Monitor concurrent EU Digital Identity Wallet and eIDAS2 working-group activity closely from month 1, and time phase three EU engagement (months 17–24) to directly feed project findings into working groups that are actively drafting specifications, maximizing influence on emerging EU-level language while aligning Danish procurement with harmonized standards.

Propose a formal joint working arrangement with an established EU-level standards body (e.g., ENISA or a eIDAS2 technical working group) in phase one, securing a seat for the project's regulatory specialist and making EU-level engagement continuous throughout the project, trading coordination overhead for upstream influence on EU specifications.

Execute Denmark-first procurement language in phase three independently, then use that language and the demonstrators as a proof-of-concept to advocate for similar EU-level requirements in month 20–24, positioning Denmark as a leadership exemplar rather than waiting for EU consensus to emerge.
levers.review: Monitoring and timing requires accurate prediction of EU body activity and risks chasing a moving target; formal joint arrangements with EU bodies add coordination complexity but guarantee venue; Denmark-first approach maximizes autonomy but risks regulatory misalignment if EU standards diverge. None address how to manage political friction if EU bodies reject or dilute language that Denmark has already embedded in procurement.

levers.name: Budget Contingency and Phase-Gate Discipline
levers.consequences: The project is budgeted at 10.5 million DKK across three phases with conditional funding (phase two and three are gated on phase one deliverables and institutional engagement). If phase one overruns or delivers weak institutional engagement, phase two funding becomes vulnerable to reallocation or cancellation, eliminating the demonstrators that provide proof-of-concept for phase three. Conversely, if phase two demonstrators succeed rapidly and phase three institutional traction appears strong, stakeholders may pressure scope expansion (production-readiness, feature richness, rapid pilot deployment) that exceeds the remaining budget and delays phase three messaging work. Budget discipline requires either strict gating (refusing scope expansion and deferring features to out-of-scope future phases) or explicit contingency reserve allocation (retaining 10–15% of budget unallocated until phase three to respond to emergent institutional opportunities).
options: Enforce strict conditional funding gates with published phase-exit criteria (phase one: published feasibility report + formal stakeholder engagement letter + documented financing plan; phase two: working demonstrators + independent security review + positive feedback from at least one regulatory stakeholder), refusing scope expansion and deferring feature requests to a post-project roadmap.

Allocate a 1.5 million DKK contingency reserve held by the project lead outside the formal phase budgets, enabling rapid response to emergent institutional opportunities (e.g., a surprise EU working-group request, an unexpected Digitaliseringsstyrelsen receptiveness, or demonstrator findings requiring urgent follow-up analysis) without derailing primary phase deliverables.

Structure phase funding with explicit overrun tolerance (e.g., allow phase one to consume up to 3.5 million DKK if institutional engagement requires additional stakeholder meetings), then correspondingly reduce phase two or three scope, making trade-offs explicit rather than hidden or deferred.
levers.review: Strict gating minimizes scope creep but may miss high-leverage institutional opportunities that require immediate response; contingency reserve adds complexity and governance risk; flexible overrun tolerance makes budgets soft and phase three scope unclear. None prevent the scenario in which phase three arrives with credible demonstrators but insufficient budget for sustained procurement influence over a 6–8 month policy window.

levers.name: Demonstrator Maturity and Certification Pathway
levers.consequences: Building non-production demonstrators on GrapheneOS or comparable platforms proves technical feasibility of standards-based authentication without Apple/Google dependency, but raises institutional expectations about production readiness and may trigger premature demand for full MitID compatibility testing. The choice of target certification level (eIDAS2 Substantial versus lower assurance) directly affects both credibility with regulators and scope creep during phase two.
options: Develop two separate demonstrators—one mobile-centric on GrapheneOS achieving eIDAS Substantial-level assurance through external security review, and one browser-based fallback requiring only browser APIs and no OS-level trust signals—to establish that platform-neutral paths exist at different assurance tiers without forcing a single unified architecture.

Build a single integrated demonstrator targeting eIDAS Substantial certification and seeking formal European Digital Identity Wallet compatibility testing, accepting longer timelines and higher technical overhead in exchange for direct regulatory recognition and clearer EU-level standards alignment.

Prioritize a minimalist hardware-token-based fallback demonstrator (FIDO2 over NFC or USB) that deliberately avoids mobile OS dependency entirely, trading off ease-of-citizen-use for absolute clarity that the fallback path is genuinely independent of Apple, Google, and future platform policy changes.
levers.review: Demonstrator scope directly trades maturity against speed; the unaddressed gap is how to prevent phase-two scope creep when institutional stakeholders conflate demonstrator feasibility with deployment-readiness.

levers.name: Resilience Framing Versus Platform-Neutrality Language
levers.consequences: Emphasizing supplier-concentration risk, continuity-of-service exposure, and contingency-planning rationales (rather than anti-platform ideology or privacy critique) appeals to risk-management stakeholders and procurement authorities, but may dilute the underlying digital-sovereignty argument and cede moral authority to incumbent operators who claim they are already resilient. The framing choice shapes which coalitions mobilize and which institutional decision-makers feel empowered to act.
options: Lead with supplier-concentration and geopolitical-contingency risk language in all policy documents and procurement engagement, positioning platform neutrality as a necessary consequence of resilience rather than an ideological goal, and restrict digital-sovereignty framing to internal coalition communications and civil-society audiences.

Maintain parallel messaging—resilience and contingency arguments for institutional and procurement stakeholders, combined with explicit digital-sovereignty and democratic-accountability arguments in parallel public and EU-facing communications—accepting the complexity cost of message coherence in exchange for broader coalition appeal.

Anchor the entire project narrative on a single formal risk assessment (e.g., 'Danish Digital Identity Contingency and Supplier Concentration Report') published in month three of phase one, establishing a neutral, evidence-based baseline that all subsequent messaging and coalition engagement references, reducing the perception of selective framing.
levers.review: Resilience framing gains institutional traction but may obscure sovereignty concerns; the unaddressed gap is whether contingency risk alone justifies major architectural changes absent an acute crisis.

levers.name: AltID Engagement Timing and Influence Depth
levers.consequences: AltID's eIDAS2 wallet rollout creates a design window where platform-neutral requirements can be incorporated before the next identity stack hardens incumbent dependencies, but the rollout timeline may not align with this project's phase gates, and the project has no formal authority over AltID's architecture. Early engagement risks being dismissed as premature; late engagement finds decisions already locked in. The depth of sought influence (advisory input versus formal procurement language) affects both political feasibility and institutional resistance.
options: Pursue formal procurement advisory-board or technical working-group membership in AltID from month six onward, positioning the project as a standards and resilience expert and building incremental influence over months 12–20 when wallet design decisions crystallize, accepting slower formal traction in exchange for sustainable institutional presence.

Submit a detailed 'platform-neutral procurement requirements' white paper to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen by month four, styled as formal policy input rather than advocacy, with the explicit goal of shaping the AltID procurement RFP language before month eight, accepting higher institutional friction if the proposal is perceived as prescriptive rather than consultative.

Deliberately de-couple from AltID decision timelines in phase two and three; instead, anchor the project's influence through EU-level eIDAS2 wallet harmonization working groups and standards bodies, positioning Danish advocacy as part of broader European resilience and interoperability discussions, with the expectation that EU-level requirements cascade back into Danish procurement by month 20–24.
levers.review: Early AltID engagement risks dismissal; late engagement misses the design window; the unaddressed gap is how to time influence when AltID's own decision schedule and phase-gate discipline are unknown.

levers.name: Coalition Cohesion and Incentive Alignment
levers.consequences: Building a coalition spanning civil-society privacy advocates, security researchers, contingency-planning stakeholders, and sympathetic Folketinget members creates political credibility and distributed influence, but members have competing priorities: privacy advocates prioritize data protection, security researchers prioritize technical standards, and government insiders prioritize procurement speed. Disagreement over messaging, timeline, or technical detail can fragment the coalition and reduce institutional impact.
options: Establish a formal steering committee with written charter (month two) defining decision rules, messaging guidelines, and escalation paths, with rotating lead responsibility across constituencies (civil society lead months 2–8, researcher lead months 9–16, government-liaison lead months 17–24), ensuring no single faction dominates and incentives remain aligned.

Create three sub-coalitions around distinct outcomes: a technical standards group focused on eIDAS harmonization, a resilience and contingency group focused on supplier-concentration risk, and a digital-sovereignty and democratic-accountability group focused on public messaging, allowing each to operate semi-autonomously while coordinating through monthly cross-group briefings.

Keep the coalition loosely federated with only an informal coordination email list and monthly video calls, avoiding formal governance overhead and reducing the risk of bureaucratic friction or decision paralysis, but establish a lead partner organization (e.g., the project's host institution) as the binding anchor for continuity if individual members' priorities shift.
levers.review: Formal governance ensures alignment but introduces overhead and reduces coalition flexibility; informal coordination avoids bureaucracy but risks fragmentation when priorities diverge.

levers.name: External Security Review and Public Credibility
levers.consequences: Engaging a recognized external security firm or academic lab to review the demonstrators and feasibility work before phase-three publication establishes technical credibility with regulators and incumbent operators, but external review adds 8–12 weeks and significant cost (typically 0.5–1.0 million DKK), and reviewers may flag contingencies or limitations that complicate procurement advocacy. The timing and scope of review (demonstrators only, versus full feasibility report, versus ongoing assurance) directly affects both cost and institutional weight.
options: Commission a formal security assessment of both demonstrators by an internationally recognized firm (e.g., a Big Four auditor or top-tier security lab) in months 13–15, timed to completion before phase-three procurement engagement, and explicitly publish the assessment (redacted only for operational security) to create a third-party credibility barrier against incumbent operator dismissal.

Arrange a series of rolling peer reviews and expert workshops (months 10–18) with invited security researchers, eIDAS compliance experts, and MitID operators themselves, documenting all feedback in a transparent 'responses to expert input' document rather than commissioning a single formal report, reducing cost while building apparent institutional buy-in.

Delay external review until month 20, after demonstrators are complete and the feasibility report is drafted, allowing the project to incorporate early internal feedback and reduce the scope of formal review to validation of claimed technical properties rather than full architecture assessment, reducing cost and timeline risk at the expense of delayed institutional credibility.
levers.review: Early formal review builds credibility but adds cost and timeline pressure; late review reduces cost but delays credibility when institutional decisions are already made.

levers.name: Institutional Overhead and Workspace Governance
levers.consequences: The project requires a physical base in Copenhagen with access-controlled workspace appropriate for security-sensitive digital identity research and stakeholder meetings. Workspace type (dedicated facility versus distributed office space), governance model (project-controlled versus host-institution-controlled), and overhead allocation (separate budget line versus absorbed by host institution) directly affect both operational security and budget predictability. Insufficient overhead planning creates friction in month 8–10 when phase-two demonstrator work intensifies and stakeholder access and document-control requirements become critical.
options: Establish a dedicated, access-controlled research facility (leased or hosted at a single Copenhagen institution) under project governance, with formal document-classification protocols, visitor sign-in, and segregated demonstration-environment infrastructure, incurring approximately 0.6–0.8 million DKK over 24 months in overhead, but ensuring operational security and reducing dependence on host-institution administrative capacity.

Negotiate embedded workspace within the host institution's existing secure research or innovation facility, operating under host-institution security policies and governance, reducing dedicated overhead to approximately 0.2–0.3 million DKK (utilities and local staffing support) but accepting delays in decisions or access changes if host-institution priorities shift.

Distribute team members across multiple institutional locations (university labs, independent research facility, temporary co-working spaces for meetings) without a single dedicated facility, minimizing overhead cost but requiring explicit remote-work protocols, encrypted document repositories, and scheduled in-person coordination windows (e.g., bi-weekly meetings in Copenhagen), increasing operational friction and coordination overhead.
levers.review: Dedicated facility ensures security and operational control but adds fixed cost; distributed model reduces overhead but increases coordination friction during demonstrator development.

levers.name: EU Standards Alignment and Temporal Scope of Advocacy
levers.consequences: Engaging European Digital Identity Wallet working groups and eIDAS2 harmonization forums (months 10–24) can amplify Danish procurement influence by aligning it with broader EU resilience and interoperability requirements, but European standards development is slow and outcomes are uncertain, and linking the project's success criteria to EU-level language creates dependency on processes outside the project's control. The choice of whether to pursue EU engagement in parallel with or sequentially after Danish institutional engagement directly affects both timeline risk and credibility positioning.
options: Initiate EU-level standards engagement in month six (parallel with phase-one feasibility work), positioning Denmark as a leading voice on platform-neutral resilience and interoperability, with the explicit goal of contributing language to official European Digital Identity Wallet materials by month 20, accepting longer timelines and lower certainty of Danish procurement impact in exchange for broader strategic influence.

Pursue Danish institutional and AltID engagement intensively in phase two and early phase three (months 9–20), and only if that engagement shows weak traction by month 16 pivot to EU-level standards forums as a secondary channel for influence, reducing timeline risk for Danish outcomes but potentially arriving at EU forums too late to shape emerging standards documents.

Focus exclusively on Danish procurement and institutional influence in all three phases, treating EU-level engagement as coordination and information-sharing (attending working groups but not leading initiatives), and measure success on Danish outcomes alone, accepting that broader European impact is uncertain but reducing the project's exposure to external standards-development timelines.
levers.review: Early EU engagement amplifies voice but creates timeline dependency on slow European processes; the unaddressed gap is how to sequence Danish institutional impact and EU influence without diluting effort across two parallel tracks.

levers.name: Phase-Gate Contingency and Scope De-Escalation Triggers
levers.consequences: The project is gated at months 8 and 16, with conditional funding and explicit scope-reduction language ('if formal traction with AltID is weak by month 16, phase three should de-scope'). This discipline prevents budget overrun and scope creep but requires defining operationally clear triggers for de-escalation (e.g., 'no written response from Digitaliseringsstyrelsen by month 10' or 'demonstrator completion delayed beyond month 15') and committing to actual scope cuts when triggers are met. Weak trigger definitions or decision-maker reluctance to enforce scope cuts undermines the entire phase-gate model.
options: Establish formal, publicly documented phase-gate criteria in month one (e.g., 'phase two funding requires publication of feasibility report AND documented meeting with at least two Digitaliseringsstyrelsen stakeholders AND completion of 80 percent of phase-one deliverables by week 32'), with explicit approval authority and escalation path if criteria are not met, accepting governance overhead in exchange for credible commitment to phase gates.

Maintain flexible gate criteria reviewed monthly by the project steering committee, with criteria adjusted if emerging circumstances (e.g., unexpected government transition, AltID timeline change) warrant, reducing rigid bureaucracy but requiring strong governance discipline and clear decision rules for when adjustments are legitimate versus when they represent scope creep.

Define a single hard trigger for phase-three scope reduction ('if AltID procurement decision is finalized before month 14, phase three shifts entirely to EU-level standards and publication work, with no attempt to influence Danish procurement'), and commit that all other phase-gate reviews are advisory rather than funding-contingent, reducing decision burden but risking institutional drift if phase-one or phase-two deliverables are weak.
levers.review: Formal gates prevent scope creep but require discipline in execution; the unaddressed gap is defining objective triggers that distinguish legitimate scope adjustment from gate-breaking scope expansion.

Be concise and grounded — only cite specific numbers if the project context provides evidence for them. Do not fabricate percentages or cost estimates. Target length: 2–4 sentences.
   - Options MUST:

Plan:
Denmark's national digital identity infrastructure currently depends in practice on Apple iOS and Google Android for broad citizen access to essential services such as banking, tax filing, healthcare portals, and public administration. This dependency is not limited to app-store distribution. MitID's anti-fraud and app-integrity model relies on platform-controlled signals concerning approved installation channels and device integrity, which means that critical parts of the trust model for Danish digital identity are mediated by two foreign commercial platform providers. Even where direct observation of specific authentication events is not publicly documented, the current setup leaves Danish digital identity structurally dependent on platform vendors that control app availability, device trust signals, and surrounding telemetry environments. This creates not only a digital-sovereignty problem, but also a resilience and contingency problem: essential public access depends on a narrow supplier base and lacks a clearly platform-neutral fallback path.

This matters because Denmark's public-sector digital strategy for 2026–2029 explicitly calls for reduced dependence on a small number of large foreign technology suppliers and for stronger digital sovereignty. The issue should therefore not be framed only as privacy or ideology, but as a concrete public-sector risk involving supplier concentration, reduced strategic autonomy, continuity-of-service exposure, and the absence of a robust fallback authentication path if platform policies, integrity APIs, distribution terms, or geopolitical conditions change.

This project does not attempt to build and certify a production-ready replacement for MitID within the current trust framework. That would be unrealistic. The MitID ecosystem is conservative, certification-heavy, and tightly coupled to Apple/Google platform integrity signals. Instead, the project's objective is to establish the technical, regulatory, and political basis for formal platform-neutral access requirements and a certified fallback authentication path for Danish digital identity. The primary intervention point is not retrofitting MitID itself, but influencing AltID — Denmark's staged eIDAS2 wallet rollout — together with related procurement, standards, and continuity-planning decisions before the next identity stack hardens the same dependencies.

The project is structured in three phases over 24 months with a total budget of 10.5 million DKK, gated across phases (3.0 million for phase one, 4.0 million for phase two, 3.5 million for phase three). The higher budget reflects the need for credible technical work, policy engagement, external review, institutional overhead, and contingency capacity. Do not assume that 8 million DKK is sufficient for the same scope.

Phase one (months 1–8) is a feasibility, risk, and coalition-building phase. The technical work maps the relevant MitID dependency surface, especially platform integrity assumptions, app-distribution constraints, and the architectural conditions required for a platform-neutral or fallback trust model under eIDAS and NSIS at level "Substantial" or higher. The policy work reframes the issue in terms of resilience, continuity of service, procurement neutrality, and supplier concentration risk, while also addressing privacy and democratic accountability. In parallel, the advocacy work builds a coalition spanning civil-society organisations, privacy advocates, academic researchers, security experts, contingency-planning stakeholders, and sympathetic members of Folketinget's digital policy committee. The deliverables are: (1) a published feasibility and risk report, (2) a formal policy proposal to Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, (3) a fallback-authentication concept note oriented toward AltID and future procurement requirements, and (4) a permit/approval and stakeholder matrix with lead times, decision gates, and identified blockers. Phase one funding is unconditional.

Phase two (months 9–16) develops non-production technical demonstrators. These are not certified MitID clients and do not attempt production integration with live MitID systems. The main demonstrator authenticates against a simulated Danish public-sector identity-provider environment using open standards such as FIDO2/WebAuthn and OpenID Connect on GrapheneOS or one comparable privacy-respecting Android-compatible platform. A secondary demonstrator explores a browser-based or hardware-token-based fallback authentication path that reduces dependence on the mobile OS duopoly altogether. The goal is not to prove immediate deployability, but to produce credible technical evidence that secure, standards-based, fallback-capable access models are feasible without exclusive reliance on Apple or Google as trust anchors. Keep the demonstrator scope lean and defensible; do not expand into feature-rich product development. Phase two funding is conditional on phase one producing a published feasibility report, at least one formal institutional engagement with Digitaliseringsstyrelsen, the MitID operator, or a related public-sector stakeholder, and a documented financing plan covering the remainder of the project.

Phase three (months 17–24) focuses on procurement, standards, and continuity intervention around AltID and related digital identity planning. Using the feasibility report, demonstrators, and coalition built in earlier phases, the project seeks inclusion of requirements stating that Danish digital identity systems should not depend exclusively on Apple or Google app stores, platform integrity APIs, or proprietary push-notification infrastructure, and should include a platform-neutral or otherwise certified fallback access path for critical public authentication. The project also engages with relevant EU bodies and technical working groups connected to the European Digital Identity Wallet framework, with the aim of aligning Danish advocacy with broader European requirements on interoperability, portability, resilience, and reduced platform lock-in. The project's role is not to dictate architecture directly, but to create technical evidence, procurement language, and standards pressure that make supplier-neutral and fallback-capable design harder to exclude. If formal traction with AltID is weak by month 16, phase three should de-scope toward publication, coalition consolidation, and EU-facing standards input rather than pretending Danish procurement influence has been secured.

The project team should include a lead researcher in mobile security and authentication protocols, a regulatory and compliance specialist familiar with Danish and EU digital identity frameworks (including eIDAS and NSIS), a policy and public-affairs coordinator experienced in Danish digital governance and procurement processes, a technical lead for the demonstrator work, and at least one additional engineer or contractor covering web authentication, hardware-token workflows, or Linux/GrapheneOS-related implementation. The technical staffing should avoid dependence on a single specialist. Assume the project's primary physical base is in Copenhagen, Denmark, at a Danish university, independent research institution, or security-qualified R&D facility providing access-controlled workspace appropriate for security-sensitive digital identity research, development, and stakeholder meetings. Budget for institutional overhead, external security review, and limited legal/procurement support explicitly rather than treating them as absorbed costs.

Success criteria: by month 24, the project has produced a published feasibility and risk report on platform-neutral and fallback-capable Danish digital identity; delivered two working non-production demonstrators (one mobile-oriented, one browser-based or hardware-token-based fallback); secured a formal written response from Digitaliseringsstyrelsen or another relevant authority to the project's proposal; and achieved inclusion of platform-neutrality, fallback access, continuity, resilience, or supplier-concentration language in at least one official AltID-related design, policy, consultation, or procurement document. A stretch goal is that the project's EU-level engagement contributes to language in relevant European Digital Identity Wallet materials that supports platform-neutral access or certified fallback mechanisms. Do not use consumer adoption rates as a primary KPI for this project, because it is not shipping a production identity product.

Pick a realistic scenario that accounts for institutional inertia, regulatory friction, incumbent resistance, financing uncertainty, and the likelihood that convenience arguments will be used against platform-neutral alternatives. Do not assume constructive cooperation from existing operators. The primary lever is not technical disruption for its own sake, but the combination of resilience framing, procurement intervention, standards pressure, and credible technical demonstration.
